notes.definition: A pyramid of biomass is a diagram, drawn to scale, that shows the relative amount of biomass (mass of living material) at each trophic level of a food chain. Trophic level 1 (the producers) is always the bottom bar.
explanation: Biomass is the mass of living material in organisms. A pyramid of biomass shows how much biomass there is at each trophic level of a food chain. Each trophic level is drawn as a horizontal bar, and the width of each bar represents the biomass at that level. The bars are stacked on top of each other, centred, with trophic level 1 (producers) at the bottom, then primary consumers, secondary consumers and so on up to the top carnivore.

Biomass data for pyramids are usually given per unit area, for example grams per square metre (g/m²), so that different trophic levels in the same habitat can be compared fairly. To construct an accurate pyramid you must draw every bar using the same scale. First choose a scale that makes the widest bar (the producers) fit on the page, for example 1 cm = 100 g/m². Then divide each biomass value by the scale value to find the width of its bar. Label each bar with the organism or trophic level.

Pyramids of biomass are almost always pyramid shaped: each bar is narrower than the one below it. This is because biomass is lost at each step of a food chain. Not all of an organism is eaten, not everything eaten is absorbed (some is egested as faeces), and much of the absorbed material is used in respiration and lost as carbon dioxide and water. Only about 10% of the biomass at one level ends up in the level above.

Pyramids of biomass let you compare food chains and ecosystems. A very narrow top bar shows that only a small amount of biomass is available, so only a small population of the top carnivore can be supported. Comparing the widths of neighbouring bars shows what proportion of biomass is transferred. For example, if the producers have 2000 g/m² and the herbivores have 180 g/m², then 180 ÷ 2000 × 100 = 9% of the biomass was transferred.

A pyramid of biomass shows mass, not numbers of organisms. A single oak tree can feed thousands of caterpillars, but the oak has a far greater mass than all the caterpillars together. So in a pyramid of biomass the oak still forms the widest bar at the bottom, and the shape is still a pyramid.
keyFacts: A pyramid of biomass shows the relative amount of biomass at each trophic level of a food chain.
Trophic level 1 (producers) is always at the bottom of the pyramid.
The width of each bar represents the biomass at that trophic level.
All bars must be drawn to the same scale to make an accurate pyramid.
Biomass is usually given per unit area, for example g/m².
Biomass decreases at each trophic level, so the bars get narrower towards the top.
Only about 10% of the biomass at one trophic level is transferred to the next.
Bar width = biomass ÷ biomass represented by 1 cm on the scale.

keyTerms.definition: The mass of living material in an organism or group of organisms.
A scale diagram of stacked bars showing the relative amount of biomass at each trophic level, with producers at the bottom.
The feeding position of an organism in a food chain, numbered from 1 (producers).
The value that one unit of bar width represents, for example 1 cm = 100 g/m². It must be the same for every bar.
A plant or alga that makes its own food by photosynthesis; it forms the bottom bar of the pyramid.

equations.name: Efficiency of biomass transfer
equations.formula: efficiency (%) = biomass transferred to the next level ÷ biomass available at the previous level × 100
equations.symbols: efficiency = (biomass in higher level ÷ biomass in lower level) × 100

workedExamples.title: Working out bar widths
workedExamples.question: A food chain has these biomasses: grass 800 g/m², grasshoppers 90 g/m², frogs 8 g/m². Using a scale of 1 cm = 100 g/m², calculate the width of each bar.
steps: Divide each biomass by the value of 1 cm: width = biomass ÷ 100.
Frogs: 8 ÷ 100 = 0.08 cm (less than 1 mm, so draw it as a very thin bar).
workedExamples.answer: Grass 8 cm, grasshoppers 0.9 cm, frogs 0.08 cm.

workedExamples.title: Reading biomass from a bar
workedExamples.question: On a pyramid drawn with a scale of 1 cm = 50 g/m², the bar for primary consumers is 2.4 cm wide. Calculate the biomass of the primary consumers.
steps: Biomass = bar width × value of 1 cm.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a scale
workedExamples.question: Producers have a biomass of 3000 g/m². A student wants the producer bar to be 12 cm wide. Calculate the scale, then the width of the bar for secondary consumers with a biomass of 45 g/m².
steps: Value of 1 cm = 3000 ÷ 12 = 250 g/m², so the scale is 1 cm = 250 g/m².
Convert to mm to help draw it: 0.18 cm × 10 = 1.8 mm.
workedExamples.answer: Scale 1 cm = 250 g/m²; secondary consumer bar = 0.18 cm (1.8 mm).

workedExamples.title: Calculating transfer from a pyramid
workedExamples.question: In a pyramid of biomass the producers have 2000 g/m² and the primary consumers have 180 g/m². Calculate the percentage of biomass transferred.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a pyramid of biomass shows the number of organisms at each level.
misconceptions.right: In fact it shows the mass of living material. One oak tree can support thousands of caterpillars, but its bar is still the widest because its biomass is far greater.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often draw the bars roughly, making each one 'a bit smaller' than the one below.
misconceptions.right: In fact an accurate pyramid uses the same scale for every bar, so a level with one tenth of the biomass has a bar one tenth as wide.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often put the top carnivore at the bottom because it is the biggest animal.
misconceptions.right: In fact trophic level 1 (producers) always goes at the bottom, whatever the size of the individual organisms.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the biomass 'disappears' or is destroyed between levels.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is lost from the food chain: some is not eaten, some is egested in faeces, and much is used in respiration and released as carbon dioxide and water.

realWorld: Ecologists compare pyramids of biomass from different years to see whether a habitat such as a lake is losing producers, for example after pollution.
Pyramids of biomass help explain why large predators such as tigers or eagles have small populations and need large territories: there is very little biomass at the top level.
Farmers and food planners use the same idea to show why more people can be fed per hectare from crops than from livestock.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic (constructing and interpreting pyramids of biomass) is in separate Biology (8461) only. It is not assessed in Combined Science Trilogy (8464).
examTips: When drawing a pyramid, use a ruler, choose one scale for all bars, centre the bars and label each with the organism or trophic level.
Show the scale working: width = biomass ÷ value of 1 cm. Examiners award marks for the method even if a bar is drawn slightly wrong.
If asked why the pyramid is pyramid shaped, give specific losses (egestion, respiration, parts not eaten), not just 'energy is lost'.
Check units: biomass is usually in g/m² or kg/m². Keep all values in the same unit before comparing or calculating.
summary: A pyramid of biomass shows the relative biomass at each trophic level.
Producers (trophic level 1) are always the bottom bar.
Bar widths are drawn to the same scale: width = biomass ÷ scale value.
Biomass decreases at each level, so bars get narrower towards the top.
Biomass is lost through parts not eaten, egestion and respiration.
Comparing bar widths shows the percentage of biomass transferred between levels.

questions.question: Which trophic level is always drawn at the bottom of a pyramid of biomass?
options: Apex predators
Producers
Herbivores
Decomposers
markScheme: 1 mark: producers
questions.explanation: Trophic level 1, the producers, is always the bottom bar. Herbivores come next. Apex predators are at the top, and decomposers are not shown in a pyramid of biomass for a food chain.

questions.question: In a pyramid of biomass, what does the width of each bar represent?
options: The biomass at that trophic level
The number of organisms at that trophic level
The amount of light energy reaching the habitat
The size of one individual organism
markScheme: 1 mark: the biomass at that trophic level
questions.explanation: Bar width is proportional to the total mass of living material at that level. It is not the number of organisms, and not the size of one individual.

questions.question: Why does a pyramid of biomass usually get narrower towards the top?
options: There are more organisms at the top
Top carnivores have the largest total biomass
There is less biomass at each higher trophic level
The top bars are drawn using a different scale
markScheme: 1 mark: there is less biomass at each higher trophic level
questions.explanation: Biomass is lost at each step of the food chain, so each level has less than the level below. All bars must use the same scale.

questions.question: Which unit is most suitable for the biomass values used to construct a pyramid of biomass?
options: °C
kJ
cm³
g/m²
markScheme: 1 mark: g/m²
questions.explanation: Biomass is a mass, usually measured per unit area so levels can be compared: g/m². kJ is a unit of energy, cm³ of volume and °C of temperature.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a food chain.
How many bars would a pyramid of biomass for this food chain have?

markScheme: 1 mark: 4
questions.explanation: There is one bar for each trophic level, and this chain has four trophic levels.

questions.question: Which data are needed to construct a pyramid of biomass for a food chain?
options: The number of individuals of each species
The average length of each organism
The mass of organisms at each trophic level per unit area
Only the number of trophic levels
markScheme: 1 mark: the mass of organisms at each trophic level per unit area
questions.explanation: A pyramid of biomass needs the biomass of each trophic level, measured over the same area. Counting individuals would give the number of organisms, not their mass.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a pyramid of biomass for a food chain.
The top bar is very narrow compared with the bar below it.
Which is the best conclusion?

options: Only a small amount of biomass is available at the top level, so only a small population of the top carnivore can be supported
The top carnivore must be a very small animal
The top carnivore reproduces very quickly
The producers in this food chain have very little biomass
markScheme: 1 mark: only a small amount of biomass at the top level, so only a small population can be supported
questions.explanation: Bar width shows total biomass at a level, not the size of individuals. A narrow top bar means little biomass reached that level, which can support only a few top carnivores.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the biomass at each trophic level in a pond food chain.
Which statement is correct?
options: The biomass of minnows is greater than the biomass of water fleas
The perch have the greatest biomass
Biomass doubles at each trophic level
The biomass of water fleas is one tenth of the biomass of algae
markScheme: 1 mark: the biomass of water fleas is one tenth of the biomass of algae
questions.explanation: 40 ÷ 400 = 0.1, which is one tenth. Minnows (5 g/m²) have less biomass than water fleas, perch have the least, and biomass decreases at each level rather than doubling.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the bottom two bars of two pyramids of biomass, P and Q.
Both pyramids are drawn to the same scale.
In both pyramids the producer bar is 10 cm wide. The herbivore bar is 0.6 cm wide in P and 1.2 cm wide in Q.
Which conclusion is correct?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 480 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif"><rect x="20" y="90" width="200" height="34" fill="#86efac" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2"/><rect x="114" y="56" width="12" height="34" fill="#fde68a" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="120" y="145" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Producers</text><text x="120" y="40" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Herbivores</text><line x1="120" y1="44" x2="120" y2="54" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" stroke-opacity="0.6"/><text x="120" y="20" font-size="14" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Pyramid P</text><rect x="260" y="90" width="200" height="34" fill="#86efac" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2"/><rect x="348" y="56" width="24" height="34" fill="#fde68a" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="360" y="145" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Producers</text><text x="360" y="40" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Herbivores</text><line x1="360" y1="44" x2="360" y2="54" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" stroke-opacity="0.6"/><text x="360" y="20" font-size="14" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Pyramid Q</text></svg>

options: P has more producer biomass than Q
A smaller percentage of producer biomass is transferred to herbivores in P than in Q
The herbivores in Q are larger animals than those in P
P must have more trophic levels than Q
markScheme: 1 mark: a smaller percentage of producer biomass is transferred to herbivores in P
questions.explanation: The producer bars are equal, so the producer biomass is the same. P transfers 0.6 ÷ 10 × 100 = 6% and Q transfers 1.2 ÷ 10 × 100 = 12%. Bar width says nothing about the size of individual animals or the number of levels.

questions.question:
A student draws a pyramid of biomass using a scale of 1 cm = 100 g/m².
The producers have a biomass of 850 g/m².
Calculate the width of the producer bar.
markScheme: 1 mark: 8.5 cm
questions.explanation: Width = biomass ÷ value of 1 cm = 850 ÷ 100 = 8.5 cm.

questions.question:
On a pyramid of biomass drawn with a scale of 1 cm = 50 g/m², the bar for primary consumers is 2.4 cm wide.
Calculate the biomass of the primary consumers.
markScheme: 1 mark: 120 g/m²
questions.explanation: Biomass = bar width × value of 1 cm = 2.4 × 50 = 120 g/m². Dividing instead of multiplying (giving 0.048) is a common error.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the biomass of two trophic levels in a food chain.
Calculate the percentage of the producer biomass that is transferred to the primary consumers.
markScheme: 1 mark: 9%
questions.explanation: Efficiency = biomass transferred ÷ biomass available × 100 = 180 ÷ 2000 × 100 = 9%. This is close to the typical figure of about 10%.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the biomass at each trophic level in a food chain.
How many times greater is the biomass of the producers than the biomass of the secondary consumers?
questions.explanation: 1500 ÷ 12 = 125, so the producer bar would be 125 times wider than the secondary consumer bar.

questions.question:
In a woodland, the secondary consumers have a biomass of 15 g/m². Exactly 10% of the biomass of the primary consumers is transferred to the secondary consumers.
Calculate the biomass of the primary consumers.
markScheme: 1 mark: 150 g/m²
questions.explanation: If 10% of the primary consumer biomass equals 15 g/m², then the total is 15 ÷ 0.10 = 150 g/m². Multiplying 15 by 0.1 (giving 1.5) works in the wrong direction.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the biomass at each trophic level in a food chain.
Calculate the percentage of the total biomass in this food chain that is in the producers.
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: Add all levels first to get 2650 g/m², then 2400 ÷ 2650 × 100 = 90.566... which is 90.6% to 3 significant figures. Most biomass in a food chain is in the producers.

questions.question:
A student is drawing a pyramid of biomass.
Table 1 shows the biomass of two of the trophic levels.
The student wants the producer bar to be 12 cm wide.
Calculate the width of the bar for the secondary consumers.
markScheme: 1 mark: scale = 3000 ÷ 12 = 250 g/m² per cm
1 mark: 0.18 cm
questions.explanation: First find the scale: 1 cm represents 3000 ÷ 12 = 250 g/m². Then width = 45 ÷ 250 = 0.18 cm (1.8 mm). Check: 0.18 × 250 = 45.

questions.question:
The producers in a food chain have a biomass of 600 g/m². The primary consumers have a biomass of 60 g/m².
Calculate the biomass that is not transferred from the producers to the primary consumers.
questions.explanation: The biomass not transferred is the difference between the two levels: 600 − 60 = 540 g/m². Most of the biomass does not pass to the next level.

questions.question: State which trophic level is drawn at the bottom of a pyramid of biomass.
markScheme: 1 mark: trophic level 1 / producers
questions.explanation: The producers (plants and algae) are always the bottom bar.

questions.question: Describe what a pyramid of biomass shows.
markScheme: 1 mark: the (relative) amount of biomass / mass of living material
1 mark: at each trophic level of a food chain
questions.explanation: A pyramid of biomass compares the biomass at each trophic level, drawn as bars to scale.

questions.question: State what happens to the amount of biomass at each trophic level as you go up a food chain.
markScheme: 1 mark: it decreases
questions.explanation: Biomass decreases at each higher trophic level because biomass is lost between levels.

questions.question: Give two features of an accurately drawn pyramid of biomass.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: all bars drawn to the same scale / width proportional to biomass; producers (trophic level 1) at the bottom; bars stacked and centred; each bar labelled with organism or trophic level
questions.explanation: Accuracy depends on scale: every bar must use the same scale so the widths can be compared fairly.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows biomass data for a food chain in a field and a food chain in a pond.
Describe two differences between the pyramids of biomass for these two food chains.
acceptedAnswers: field producer biomass is twice the pond
field has more biomass at level 2
markScheme: 1 mark: the pond pyramid has more trophic levels / four bars compared with three
1 mark: the field has greater producer biomass (twice as much) / greater biomass at level 2 / level 3
questions.explanation: Compare like with like: number of bars, and the biomass at the same trophic level. Field producers 1200 g/m² are twice the pond's 600 g/m².

questions.question: One oak tree supports 5000 caterpillars. Explain why the pyramid of biomass for oak → caterpillar is still pyramid shaped.
acceptedAnswers: mass of tree greater than all caterpillars
markScheme: 1 mark: a pyramid of biomass shows mass, not number of organisms
1 mark: the mass of the oak tree is much greater than the total mass of all the caterpillars
questions.explanation: Even though there is only one tree, its biomass is enormous compared with the caterpillars, so the producer bar is the widest.

questions.question: Explain why the biomass at each trophic level in a pyramid of biomass is less than the biomass at the level below.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any three: not all of the organism is eaten (e.g. roots, bones); not all ingested material is absorbed / some is egested as faeces; much absorbed material is used in respiration; lost as carbon dioxide and water; some lost as waste such as urea in urine
questions.explanation: Only about 10% of biomass passes to the next level. Specific losses earn marks; 'energy is used up' alone is too vague.

questions.question: Use the idea of a pyramid of biomass to suggest why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels.
acceptedAnswers: too little biomass at the top
not enough biomass for a population
markScheme: 1 mark: biomass decreases at each trophic level (only about 10% transferred)
1 mark: so after a few levels there is too little biomass to support a population of another level
questions.explanation: Each bar is roughly one tenth of the one below, so the top bars quickly become tiny. Eventually there is not enough biomass to support a further trophic level.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows biomass data for a food chain.
A student used a scale of 1 cm = 100 g/m² to draw a pyramid of biomass.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the biomass at each trophic level in a food chain.
Describe how you would construct an accurate pyramid of biomass from these data.
Explain the shape of the pyramid you would expect.
markScheme: Indicative content (construction):
draw one horizontal bar for each trophic level
grass (producer, level 1) at the bottom, then grasshoppers, frogs, snakes at the top
choose one scale for all bars so the widest bar fits, e.g. 1 cm = 200 g/m²
width = biomass ÷ scale value, e.g. 8 cm, 0.75 cm, 0.07 cm, 0.006 cm
bars stacked and centred, drawn with a ruler, each labelled
Indicative content (explanation):
bars get narrower at each level: biomass decreases
only about 10% of biomass transferred between levels (here about 9%)
not all of each organism is eaten
some material egested as faeces / not absorbed
much used in respiration, lost as carbon dioxide and water
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear method using a consistent scale with correct order, and a well explained shape with specific losses.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct method and some explanation of the shape.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant points, e.g. producers at bottom or bars get smaller, with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Strong answers link construction (one scale for all bars) with explanation (specific causes of biomass loss). Calculating example widths shows understanding of scale.

questions.question: Describe what a pyramid of biomass shows about a food chain and explain how it can be used to compare the transfer of biomass between trophic levels.
markScheme: Indicative content:
shows the relative amount of biomass at each trophic level
producers / level 1 at the bottom
bar width proportional to biomass, all to the same scale
bars get narrower towards the top because biomass is lost
compare widths of neighbouring bars to find the proportion transferred
efficiency = biomass at higher level ÷ biomass at lower level × 100
typically about 10% transferred
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of the pyramid and how bar widths are used to calculate or compare transfer.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic description, e.g. shows biomass, producers at the bottom.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Because every bar uses the same scale, the ratio of two bar widths equals the ratio of their biomasses, so the pyramid lets you calculate the percentage transferred.
